![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14169381/assets/f1a62bcd57c146902eb55f4a3a631cce69b743c9a3ff7bef659da392a5690476.svg)
Consider the matrix $A$ shown above.
Which of the following statements are true?

I. $a_{11}=-6$ and $\det(A) \lt 0$

II. $\mathbf{x}^T \! A \, \mathbf{x}$ is negative-definite

III. $A$ is positive-definite
question.worked_solution:
Let $\Delta_i$ for $i=1,2,\ldots,n$  denote the principal minors of an $n \times n$ matrix $A.$ Then, according to Sylvester's criterion, the quadratic form $\mathbf{x}^T \! A \, \mathbf{x}$ (as well as the matrix $A$) is 

- positive-definite if and only if $\Delta_i > 0$ for all $i=1,2,\ldots,n,$

- negative-definite if and only if, for all $i=1,2,\ldots,n,$ we have $\Delta_i <          0$ when $i$ is odd, and $\Delta_i > 0$ when $i$ is even.

With that in mind, let's examine each of the statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, $a_{11}=-6.$ Expanding $\det(A)$ along the top row, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =|\begin{aligned}-6 & -5 & 1 \\ 5 & -2 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =(-6)|\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}|-(-5)|\begin{aligned}5 & 2 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}|+1\cdot |\begin{aligned}5 & -2 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =(-6)(-2)+(5)(-7)+12 \\  & =-11.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true, while statement III is false. Notice the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Δ}_{1} & ={a}_{11}=-6<0 \\ {Δ}_{2} & =|\begin{aligned}-6 & -5 \\ 5 & -2\end{aligned}|=37>0 \\ {Δ}_{3} & =|A|=-11<0\end{aligned}
$$

So, by Sylvester's criterion, the quadratic form $\mathbf{x}^T \! A \, \mathbf{x},$ and the matrix $A,$ are negative-definite.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."
